newsitem.title: THAILAND: Esso sees Thai oil deficit in 5 years.
newsitem.headline: Esso sees Thai oil deficit in 5 years.

text.p: Oil demand in Thailand is expected to grow and push the current balanced supply/demand situation into deficit again in five years, a senior Esso official said on Tuesday.

"Thailand's oil demand/supply is basically in balance at the moment...But with economy continuing to grow, Thailand will move back into net importing position sometime in the next five years," David H. Ledlie, chairman and managing director of Esso (Thailand) PLC, told Reuters.
He said his firm, an affiliate of U.S. oil major Exxon Corp, had no plans to increase exports despite rising local supply as it was confident about the prospects for strong local demand.
"Thailand's economic fundamentals remain strong. The economy is still going fast and energy demand is still growing quite rapidly," Ledlie added.
Esso (Thailand) is currently operating a 145,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) oil refinery. Thailand's local refining capacity at present is 760,000 bpd.
But poor refining margins and slower demand forced the Esso refinery to cut crude runs for the first time by 10-15 percent recently.
Ledlie described the cut as a "short-term" measure. He forecast that demand would pick up in November and December after the rainy season had ended.
But he declined to say when the refinery would return to full capacity.
"I think this is a short-term situation, reflecting some indigestion in the region and in Thailand in absorbing the new refining capacity that comes on stream," he said.
"We see demand picking up in November and December. But again, it depends on the economy of the day and we will run our refinery to match." he added.
Although Ledlie said Esso did not rule out plans to expand the facility in the future, it had no plans to do so now.
"We will decide at the time, depending on the supply and demand balance of our time...on economic prospect," he said.

Ledlie said the company planned to continue to build 50-60 retail stations in the next five years in Thailand and would strive to maintain current market share which stood at around 22 percent despite tougher competition.
"We will continue to choose well-located, high-volume sites for the long-term prospect," he said, adding that Esso currently has about 850 retail stations in Thailand.
But despite optimism about long-term oil demand in Thailand, the company also seeks to divert into the petrochemical industry.
He said the company had some chemical operations in the eastern Sri Racha district and was developing an aromatic plant there.

"Our focus has been the broad-based downstream industry--refining and marketing...but we will continue to look aggressively at opportunity not only in downstream business but also in petrochemicals," he added.
